Prioritize building up your city first, taking any resource nodes within your area while sending scouts to fill out the map and figure out where things are. You can choose to befriend other factions by freeing their Temples, or take them over by force by killing their Lord in combat. I'd suggest allying with Water (because boats) and Air (eagles FTW)

OG Sierra development at it's finest.  Just remember the game is almost 30 yrs old, so it's not a modern interface, and there is no hand-holding.  LOMSE has never been a problem to get running (Win95 to the present 11, on non-gaming laptops/towers), and it's a natural 4:3 aspect.  It's OK to start on Easy for your first time, like most 90s games- Hard difficulty is meant to be challenging, and near-impossible for 1st-timers.  Save often, and have multiple saves slots while learning the ropes.  When you lose/die, all you can do is reload a save.  If you have replay 30 mins of turns, you will not be happy.
 
Mythical/Fantasy setting.  Beautiful old-school graphics.  Elves, Dwarves, Orcs, Knights, Dragons, Giants, Necromancers, Lizardmen, Naval Ships, Kraken, Beast-riders, etc...  8 unique Faith/Races to choose from.  You choose a Warrior, Thief or Mage for your Lord.  Turn-based over-world movement around the map, real-time w/ pause for the battles (or you can auto-calculate).  Great strategic options to play different ways..  using the rock-paper-scissors style in combat (Cavalry counters Ranged, Ranged counters Infantry, Infantry counters Cavalry), decimating enemies with Magic, or just building a big army of only cavalry..  it's all viable.  Start in your land, and take-over other lands through conquest or diplomacy.  Goal of the game is the defeat the Lord of Death, who will be actively running around the world doing his own thing while you build up your kingdom.  After you beat Death, then you can play as Death in future playthroughs.  Warriors fight and rally troops in battle.  Mages do magic and research mage spells,. I know, unbelievable right?  Thieves fight, take enemy champs hostage, and can also spy on allies/enemies, gaining info about opps, or even stealing opp resources.  Semi-RPG.. Equip artifacts on your Lords & Champions, gain XP through battles and your units will level up and get stronger until they max-out, but you can't really choose any skills or stats.  Lords/Champs can train units (warriors train inf/cav, thieves train ranged, mages train mages)  Magic spells must be researched at a Mage Tower, so you have some input on what spells you want to use.  Excellent depth in the mechanics, combat, kingdom management, and replay-ability.  Not very story-heavy, but interesting setting/world-building.  Basically, you write the story with the actions you take.  
Special Edition added new upgrades for each Faith/Race, and a new game mode that is more story-based, with stories influenced by King Arthur, Beowulf, and some original stories as well.  

Although it suffers from being released in 1997, and the limitations that come along with that, I can't say enough good things about this game.  Maybe it feels a little clunky or wonky compared to newer games, but that is the same with many games from the 90s.. like Diablo, Doom or Fallout.  Once you get the hang of it, many people enjoy the nuance of these older games.  I would recommend to watch Youtube playthroughs, but there aren't many (with commentary) who know the game very well.  They can actually mislead you, because they don't understand how they won/lost a battle, or which magic spell is the most important to focus on. (Overland Movement Spell is the answer, btw)  So, you can watch them, just don't take their teachings as gospel. 
Savvy players will notice the systems at-play and will be just fine.  The rest tend to figure it out after a couple tries.  
"Easy to play, difficult to master" is best way to describe it.

I have played this game since it released, and every year or two, I go back for another round or two.  Not a big community or anything, but there are a couple helpful websites that can give you data about the combat units and the Faith/Races differences.  I just typed "LOMSE Unit Comparison" into the browser and some old site pops-up with a database you can find and compare all the stats in the game.

OK, I'm done gas-baggin.  This review has been nearly 30 years in the making.  Thank you for your time.  --  Happy Hunting  --

⚠️ Разочаровывающий опыт в "Lords of the Realm"

"Lords of the Realm" — игра, от которой ждёшь масштабных сражений, глубокой стратегии и настоящего погружения в атмосферу средневековых войн. К сожалению, на деле проект оставляет скорее негативное впечатление.

Первое, что бросается в глаза, — устаревшая графика и слабая анимация. Даже для своего времени визуальный ряд выглядит блекло, а сейчас и вовсе кажется неактуальным. Локации невыразительны, а модели юнитов и зданий не вызывают желания рассматривать их дольше пары секунд.

Геймплей тоже не радует. Управление оказывается громоздким и неудобным, а интерфейс перегружен лишними элементами, в которых легко запутаться. Искусственный интеллект противников работает странно: иногда он совершает нелогичные действия, а порой, наоборот, читает ваши ходы, что убивает интерес к тактическим манёврам.

Баланс сил в игре оставляет желать лучшего. Некоторые юниты и стратегии оказываются слишком сильными, что делает прохождение предсказуемым и скучным. Экономическая система проработана слабо: развитие поселения сводится к рутинным действиям без какой-либо глубины.

Отдельно стоит отметить слабую техническую реализацию. В игре встречаются баги, которые могут привести к вылетам или даже потере прогресса. Музыкальное сопровождение быстро приедается, а озвучка практически отсутствует.

В итоге "Lords of the Realm" не оправдывает ожиданий. Вместо увлекательной стратегии вы получаете утомительный процесс с устаревшей графикой и спорным геймплеем. Если вы ищете качественную игру про управление средневековым королевством, лучше обратить внимание на другие проекты. Эта игра вряд ли подарит вам те эмоции, на которые вы рассчитываете.

Lords of Magic: Special Edition, developed by Impressions Games and published by Rebellion, stands as one of the most ambitious strategy titles of the late 1990s—a hybrid of turn-based empire management, real-time tactical battles, and role-playing progression wrapped in a mythic fantasy world. It presents the land of Urak, a continent divided by eight elemental faiths—Life, Death, Order, Chaos, Fire, Water, Earth, and Air—all locked in eternal rivalry after the dark lord Balkoth plunged the realm into chaos. Players take the role of a chosen lord from one of these faiths and must rebuild their temple, rally armies, explore ruins, forge alliances, and ultimately bring balance back to the world. The Special Edition bundles the original game with the Legends of Urak expansion, introduces small quality-of-life improvements, and polishes some rough edges, offering a more stable version of a cult classic that has long fascinated strategy enthusiasts.

At its heart, Lords of Magic operates on two interlocking layers. The overworld map is turn-based, where players manage resources, move heroes, construct buildings, and expand influence across provinces. Cities and temples produce units, generate income, and research spells, while wandering heroes can embark on side quests or seek relics that enhance their power. When opposing armies meet, the game shifts into real-time combat, a distinctive feature that separates it from many contemporaries like Heroes of Might and Magic or Master of Magic. Battles unfold on small, enclosed maps where positioning, timing, and hero abilities make the difference between victory and annihilation. The interplay between these systems gives the game its depth: the slow, deliberate pace of empire management contrasts with the chaos of real-time combat, where a moment’s hesitation can undo hours of careful planning.

The Special Edition refines several aspects that frustrated players in the original release. Load times are noticeably shorter, resource collection and management feel smoother, and players can now access and control buildings directly from the interface rather than needing to move heroes to every structure. The diplomacy system is slightly more logical, with improved notifications and fairer trade evaluations, though it still retains a degree of unpredictability. The inclusion of a hero editor also helps mitigate the steep learning curve by allowing players to customize their starting conditions—choosing hero classes, spells, and items that better fit their preferred playstyle. These enhancements, while modest, make the game more accessible without diluting its original complexity. However, many of the underlying mechanics remain unchanged, meaning the core experience still reflects the design philosophy of its era: slow, deliberate, and often unforgiving.

One of the most notable additions in this edition is the Legends of Urak expansion, which offers a series of standalone campaigns inspired by myth and folklore. These scenarios focus on self-contained stories drawn from familiar legends—Arthurian quests, demonic uprisings, or battles among gods—each designed to test specific skills or strategies. They serve as a welcome alternative to the sprawling sandbox campaign, giving players bite-sized experiences with clear objectives. These legends also showcase the breadth of Urak’s world-building, revealing a setting that feels ancient and lived-in, populated by tribes, monsters, and deities tied to each elemental faith. It is in these smaller, narrative-driven missions that Lords of Magic’s atmosphere shines most clearly, blending the mystery of myth with the texture of tactical warfare.

Despite these strengths, Lords of Magic: Special Edition remains a game defined as much by its flaws as by its ambition. The real-time combat, while conceptually exciting, is often hampered by awkward controls, clumsy pathfinding, and inconsistent unit behavior. Armies sometimes fail to engage properly or get stuck on terrain, and battles can devolve into chaotic brawls where precision feels secondary to brute force. The early game can also be punishing, especially for players unfamiliar with the mechanics. Marauding enemy bands roam the map freely and will mercilessly destroy your holdings if left unchecked, forcing you to juggle expansion and defense with limited resources. Healing units takes several turns, slowing down momentum, and because there is no easy catch-up mechanic, an early mistake can spell long-term disaster. The pacing reflects an older, more methodical design ethos, rewarding patience and persistence rather than accessibility or convenience.

Still, for those willing to engage with its eccentricities, there is a remarkable sense of depth beneath the surface. Each faith plays differently, not only in the types of units and spells they command but also in philosophy and approach. Fire favors aggression and destruction, Life excels at healing and protection, Order emphasizes discipline, and Chaos thrives on unpredictability. This diversity ensures that no two campaigns feel entirely alike. The game also allows for multiple victory conditions, from outright conquest to religious domination or the defeat of Balkoth himself. The moral and elemental system gives the world of Urak a strong identity, one that feels distinct from other fantasy settings of its time. Combined with haunting music, darkly atmospheric art, and a sense of mysticism that permeates every corner of the world, Lords of Magic achieves a level of immersion that transcends its technical limitations.

In terms of presentation, the game shows its age but retains a certain charm. The isometric overworld has a painterly quality, while the unit sprites and battlefields evoke the feel of classic high-fantasy illustrations. The interface, though dated, is functional once mastered, and the ambient soundtrack does much to build the mood of exploration and peril. Modern players accustomed to slick interfaces and streamlined mechanics will find the experience cumbersome at first, but those with patience will discover an atmospheric world that rewards attention to detail. The overall aesthetic reinforces a sense of mythic scale, reminding players that they are not just generals commanding troops, but divine agents shaping the fate of a fractured world.

Ultimately, Lords of Magic: Special Edition is a time capsule from a different era of PC strategy design—one where ambition outweighed accessibility, and where depth often came with rough edges. It is not a game that holds your hand or forgives your mistakes, but it remains captivating in its scope and imagination. The Special Edition’s improvements make it more stable and slightly easier to navigate, but its heart is still that of a complex, challenging, and sometimes exasperating classic. For fans of grand strategy, mythic storytelling, and games that reward experimentation, it stands as a worthy relic, offering a kind of strategic freedom and world-building rarely seen today. For newcomers, it may feel archaic, but beneath the dated interface and stubborn mechanics lies a world rich with potential—a flawed masterpiece whose ambition continues to command respect decades after its release.

An old favorite that hasn't aged well. When this game was brand new I would spend many an hour munching on carrots, drinking strong black tea, and trying to win this game when I should have been studying for my college classes. The turn based strategy combined with real time battles is most welcome here, but the interface and graphics are clunky and dated. The sound effects and voices are great, but some of the design just looks silly. The dwarfs and gnomes are cute but the Nordic high elves running around on purple raptors look like She-Ra and He-Man rejects from some awful 80s cartoon. The fire giants are amusing and sound like Sean Connery voicing a kids show. To this day I still grin when I hear them blow their horn and shout "Incinerate!" I also like the "order" faction, complete with paladins, rangers, knights and crossbowmen.
The leveling and experience system was a major plus at the time of release, but still has the major problem of time. Even when I first played this game the main campaign always ended in the Sauron evil stand-in showing up and slowly swallowing everything I'd spent hours building and upgrading. Somehow I just never had enough time to build up armies and units to be able to even challenge the evil abyss big bad boss thingy  (complete with giant bats and armies of the undead). Diplomacy with other factions bounced between being formulaic and arbitrary with few formidable results.  
The magic system barely works, but was adequate at the time of release. It is a little tedious spending much time and effort on spells that barely did much until the magic units were upgraded up to or near maximum level. Even if I managed to conquer a few provinces and gather/upgrade powerful units the opposition would show up again and mop the floor with the heads of my most powerful units.
The auto calculation option for battles would primarily succeed in killing off units that I was trying to develop so most of the time it wasn't an option.      
There's an attempt at rewarding the player for exploration with a few scattered major dungeons that bring resources and characters, but they are often too far, too few, and too late. Managing resources and supplies does take effort and planning, but again the game lacks sufficient time to really build anything before the player is taken down.  
Overall this game is a forgettable Tolkien-ish high fantasy Fantasy Strategy RPG that was cool 25 years ago, but dated and clumsy these days.
It's old and clunky, yes, but this is one of my favorite games that I played when growing up, and still love playing now! Recommend for folks who like fantasy and RTS.

The basic game is straightforward: pick one of seven religions, and either a warrior, thief, or mage as your leader. Try to survive the upcoming war of conquest waged by the Death religion to sacrifice non-believers and bring the God of Death to the world of Urak. Each religion's units have different strengths and weaknesses. The mages of each faction have spells that fit their ethos. For instance, Fire has Meteor Storm, Life has Resurrection, Chaos has Reincarnation, etc. Main gameplay is turn-based strategy and overland movement, but combats/encounters are real-time with a pause button.

At the release of Lords of Magic Special Edition, a critical typo cripples one of the factions, Chaos. Since then, a LOMSE 3.0.2 community patch corrects the defect.

Players can choose to play the game unmodified, with the community patch, or enhance it with ManTerA's GS5R3 mod, which make it possible to click on the spells in your faction Report to see the details of what each spell you own does.
It also changes the spells so that Meteor Storm changes the terrain type to Lava on the square where it hits, and Earthbind actually binds non-Air flying creatures. There are a number of other changes, but gamers usually either love the GS5R3 mod, or they hate it. Community mods can also add werewolves to the Chaos faction, for those gamers that have a background in Werewolf the Apocalypse table top RPG.

Originally, LOMSE had 640x480 resolution at its original 1997 release, so LOMSE is a game which can benefit from dxwnd to change its graphics resolution. By default, LOMSE will open fullscreen, making it kind of blurry on modern monitors.

LOMSE's engine can only handle 16-bit audio. However, a community member updated and re-mastered soundtracks to eliminate audio hiss and update from 8-bit to 16-bit audio.


[b]Where is the replay value?[/b]
After you beat the Death religion, you can play again as that faction. There are also five (5) legendary campaigns from the history of the world of Urak. On the community side, the GS5R3 mod includes 8 maps. Community modders also created another 53 other maps.
LOMSE also permits playing interactively with other players across the internet, across LAN, or a null modem cable.

I played this for the first time in 2024 so the following review is not biased by any nostalgia for the game. However, it is biased by a fondness for retro games and the fantasy genre. If you enjoy retro fantasy games like myself, then this game is for you. 

Lords of Magic is an easy to learn, turn based strategy game with real time combat in which you develop your buildings, build up your army, and go out to conquer your enemies while exploring the world of Urak. The artwork and audio is stereotypical of the dark, ominous portrayal in which fantasy was represented to audiences of the 70's and 80's which creates a wonderful ambience to the game. The artwork is particularly reminiscent of the Heavy Metal franchise if you are familiar with that reference. 

Unfortunately, the gameplay is quite shallow. After one playthrough, there is not much more to experience. Nonetheless, I can see myself coming back in a year or so to relive the joy of playing this game. But even if I never play it again, I definitely got my money's worth as it currently costs less than a cup of coffee. 

Gameplay tip: the pause feature is one of the greatest tactical advantages you will have in every fight.

Updated edit: I noticed some of the negative comments talk about bugs. I have no doubt that some people may experience bugs with a retro game like this however, I did not encounter any bugs or problems running the game during my entire playthrough. Also, if you are familiar with gaming in the 80's and 90's, you will know that one did not rely on in-game tutorials. Rather, one learned the game by reading the manual, and that's the case with Lords of Magic which comes with a 242 page manual rich in lore. I wish I had bought this game back in the 90's just to get my hands on a hard copy of the original manual.

One of my favorite games that I enjoyed playing in the late 90s, I still have the CD, but my desktop PC has been dead for a few years.  I'm so happy to add this fine game to my Steam library on my laptop.

Lords of Magic has a great fantasy story with different factions whose powers are based on religions rooted in themes of the four elements, nature, chaos, order, life, and death.  Each faction must liberate their Great Temple to open up ownership of a capital.

You can either micromanage battles or let the computer handle them.  Scattered around  the map are houses, manors, statues, and caves of various levels to investigate inhabited by bands of vagabonds and brigands  to clear out.  There are also roving bands of marauders to keep you on your toes.

The graphics are very nice, quite colorful and well done for the time the game was made in.  I don't think it would be an exaggeration to say that LOM was one of the best fantasy empire building games of the 1990s.

El Lords of Magic "común" era interesante pero era una bolsa de bugs, te exasperaba por momentos de tanta cantidad de errores que muchas veces arruinaban la partida.  
Pero este "Special Edition" cambió todo. No solamente corrigió casi todos los errores que tenia sino que amplio el juego con mas unidades y mas cositas. 
Si nunca lo jugaste tal vez te parezca durisimo pero si sos de esos que se animan a los juegos viejos, dale una oportunidad. Es un clásico.
Siempre creí que este juego es un gran candidato para una remake, necesitamos este juego con la jugabilidad y los graficos actuales. Urak (el mundo donde se desarrolla) es un lugar muy interesante. 
8 facciones, cada una con su pro y contra. Lo bueno que tiene es que podes hacerte con los edificios de otras facciones y producir sus tropas. Tu ejercito puede ser un paquete de surtido Bagley con unidades de todas las facciones.

Edit: cuando vences al "malo final" (Balkoth, de la faccion Muerte) o vences a todos con él el juego termina. Logre arrinconar a Balkoth y dejarlo sin tropas y sin movimientos. Con esa premisa me dedique a limpiar el resto del mundo. Creo que fue mi ultima partida, hice todo.
